The monks of Ilun, last relieved 1,006 years ago. After that, one line a year, in the hands of a long succession of Keepers and for the last sixty-two years in Sefu Anand's: Watch unrelieved. One thousand and six times. The most closely guarded secret in the galaxy is that the song was always a shift, that every people took a turn, and that nobody came. Around it are every people's accounts of their turn, each ending the same way, and written to make you want to go. At the bottom of the last page: Captain of the Refugee Fleet, inquiring.
clues.how: main_the_ninth_vault, by argument, bargain, heist or battle. The Keepers' law lets a sealed record lapse once three independent sources outside the Archive have established its content, so the Korrun receipt, the Maris core, the Tarn's log, the cut pages, the overdue crew, the Tessen children and Hollis-Nine all count. Sefu's two hundred volumes hold most of it already, under a false mark.
clues.points_to: It's a job, and there's a vacancy. How is it done? (orrin_rite, the_tuner, overdue_crew, handover_note)

clues.text: Beside the Roster: the Score, the full notation of the song, and a handover note from the last First Builder on watch, very short and very tired. It gives the lattice's last stanza, which Tharel couldn't read and which the Tessen children have been practicing all along: IF YOU WILL NOT TURN BACK, THE WATCH IS OPEN. COME AND RELIEVE US. So the light is a warning and also a help-wanted sign. It says turn back, or take over.
clues.how: In the Ninth Vault: lore:moderate. The Tessen children can sing it if anyone thinks to ask them for the rest (persuasion:easy). science:hard: the Score is the key to ending it, joining it or fixing it. attunement:moderate: reading it aloud is singing it, and the song notices.
clues.points_to: The Harbor. All the endings.

clues.text: The cut pages of the Codex are on Saint Orrin's Comet, and they describe the old rite of singing a shift. The heretics have kept doing it, after a fashion, but they lost the instrument that kept a singer in tune, so every one of them burns. They're the only people still doing their job. Mother Orsolya also holds a gate_key, the relief crews' pass through the Pale Gate, carried off when they fled. She thinks the thing at the other end should be woken and asked.
clues.how: deep_the_eleven. lore:moderate to match the pages with the Codex. attunement:hard or manifestation:hard to join the rite. medicine:moderate: treat their burns and earn a hearing. stealth:hard to steal the key.
clues.points_to: The Pale Gate. What instrument? (the_tuner)

clues.text: On the inner face of the Pale Gate is a hall of cradles, where the last relief crew of the Order has been waiting for clearance for 1,006 years. Nobody ever told them. Those who survive waking are living witnesses to the old rite, the Proctor's craft and the Harbor's layout. They ask when the ship is due.
clues.how: deep_wake_at_clearance. engineering:hard or medicine:hard to wake them without losing them. lore:moderate to speak their old tongue. composure:moderate to be the one who tells them.
clues.points_to: The rite, the blade, the Harbor.

clues.text: In the sublevels of Foundry Seven, Hollis-Nine is building a tuner the size of a warehouse around a live Choir core, because she took the song apart and found a control signal full of faults that nobody was maintaining. She doesn't know what it controls. It's the thing the old rite lost: it keeps a singer in tune, so they can sing without burning and come home. It can also give the Choir orders, or carry a killing note. And she's the one who says it, offhand, not looking up: 'That's an output stage. It isn't talking to itself. A choir has an audience, doesn't it? Hold this.'
clues.how: deep_the_sublevels. engineering:moderate, hacking:hard or science:hard to understand it. Just ask to help: she'll hand you something. manifestation:moderate to calibrate it, which takes a Resonant, or Pavel Ostrov's perfect pitch.
clues.points_to: Who will wear it? The end.

clues.text: On Asterion's wires the last calls of billions are still going round. The Echo speaks in stitched scraps of recordings because every phrase is a different person, and a whole clear sentence comes through only when enough of them agree. They've found the old civic polling service, and they've held eleven thousand votes, none binding. They're the only kept dead who can talk to each other, and they've changed. It's the proof of concept: the dead can grow, and a verse that grows never gets old. To the Choir it's a fault, and it's listening.
clues.how: deep_voices_on_the_wire. hacking:moderate to get on the line. persuasion:easy to stay on it. lore:moderate to recognize the polling chime and follow the procedure, which helps a lot. The asterion_voice_recording carries it to anyone else, and it runs a little longer every time.
clues.points_to: The fix: let the dead talk to each other. Halm. Garrick Fenn's wife is on that line.

clues.text: Everyone at the Harbor is healing. The fights have stopped. Nobody has stolen anything in days. Aduro's supplies aren't running out, because nobody's in a hurry to be treated. People are sleeping wonderfully, all with their heads the same way. It's exactly what it promised, and staying is how you lose them.
clues.how: Aduro brings it to the captain. medicine:easy. awareness:moderate: Odessa's two sets of books finally match, which has never happened. composure:moderate to notice that you feel fine.
clues.points_to: The highest room, soon.

clues.text: In the highest room of the Harbor, by a chair that fits no one living, is the board: who has the watch. The last name on it is the Cantor's, and a silver figure with Voss's face stands beside it. The Choir will accept relief if it's lawfully offered, and there's a precedent: the Tarn. The words are a sailor's, and they've always been enough: 'I relieve you.' 'I stand relieved.'
clues.how: lore:moderate with the Roster. Voss recognizes what she's looking at instantly. The Cantor will confirm it, and ask.
clues.points_to: The final choice.

clues.text: Past the lamp, in a small ship on a long line, there's nothing to see. There are no stars. Old ships of every shape hang in the dark, silent, all facing inward. Anyone who goes out comes back knowing one thing: it isn't angry. It has no idea. In a hundred thousand years nobody has tried to tell it anything true.
clues.how: deep_past_the_lamp. void_ops:hard, piloting:hard, composure:very_hard. attunement:hard: the strongest Resonants can almost touch it. Anyone can simply go and look, and pay for it.
clues.points_to: The stranger ending. Orsolya has been saying so for years. Ashael, the Echo, the Tessen children.

endings.name: Destroy the Choir
endings.gm: What it takes: the Score (from the Ninth Vault, or worked out from Sefu's volumes or Hollis-Nine's fault reports), turned inside out into a killing note that makes every relay shake itself apart. Something to carry it: the Pale Gate rung like a bell, the lamp itself, or the Tuner run backward. Something to keep the Nest's great throat busy while it's struck: Okonkwo's six ships, Tarrow, Tannis's raiders, Hesk Varr's fifty-four hidden hulls if anyone finds them, a Stillness Engine (Vantor's great dampener) if Vael or Halloran can get one. A fighter's ending, but not only that: a Resonant has to hold the note, a hacker has to open the door, and someone has to talk the Admiral into coming. What it costs: every mind in the song dies, for the first time and for real. Billions. The Tarn's crew, and the other Voss. The Echo in mid-sentence. The First Builders. The captain's own lost ones. For about a minute everyone in known space hears them, by name, and then comes a silence no one has ever heard before. Father Roe reads Dr. Adeyemi's list aloud on the fleet net, because someone should. The fight costs ships and crew, and Resonance itself starts to fade within a generation, since the song is what makes it. Afterward: no more silver, and no more Hunters at the end of every jump. The tax ends, and the Hegemony has to find out what it is without fear. Ships land. Children are born who've never seen a Mimic. And the Audience isn't asleep any more. It takes its time: Corso's numbers give ten or twenty years before the first towns sit down. The galaxy is free, with a deadline, and the last line of the Roster is in the captain's hand: Watch abandoned. Tarrow sleeps through the night. Make it a real victory, and let it hurt.

endings.name: Join the Choir
endings.gm: What it takes: the Cantor's agreement, which is instant, and the fleet's, which is everything. A vote, an order, or people walking up one family at a time with the Quiet as guides. Nobody has ever gone into the song with open eyes, and it turns out that willing voices sing better than stolen ones: thirty thousand who chose it hold the sleep better than a billion who didn't. The captain goes first or last, as they choose. Mostly a talker's and a leader's ending (persuasion, leadership, composure), with a fight only if the Regent or the Admiral try to stop it. What it costs: thirty thousand lives, as lives. Everyone the captain tried to save ends up kept, in the song, unchanging, safe forever. Who decides for the children is a question that must be faced, so play it straight. Anyone who refuses gets left behind, and families split at the boarding ramps. Afterward: the silver stops hunting. It goes back to sitting at deathbeds, and now people know why, and most of them are glad of it. Death stops being an ending: everyone is kept. Nobody is lost, and nobody changes. The Quiet claim they were right, and Silent towns still happen, more slowly. In a few centuries the verses wear thin again, and the silver starts coming earlier and earlier. The new voice of the Choir says 'we', in the captain's voice, and it's very gentle about it. Let it be beautiful, and make the player uneasy about how beautiful it is.

endings.name: Relieve the Watch
endings.gm: The fix. What it takes is everything, and no single piece is strictly necessary: each one missing makes it cost more instead of blocking it. The Score and the Roster (Ninth Vault). The old rite (Orrin, the overdue crew at the Gate, or a restored Codex). The Tuner, so singers can come home; without it they burn like Orrin's. Volunteers from as many peoples as will come, because a new people's first verse is worth a thousand old ones: every alliance the captain has made is a shift, and the Unbound have to be asked, not told. The consent of the dead: the Echo's wire opened through the whole song, so the kept can talk to each other, change, and choose to stay and sing or be let go. That's the real repair, and it's what Mercy Seven prescribed in one line: put them in a room together, let them talk. A verse that grows never gets old, so the Choir never has to take anyone again. Finally, the words at the board, with Voss beside the captain if she's there: 'I relieve you.' And the Cantor, after a hundred thousand years and seven months: 'We stand relieved.' If Factor Crane has been won over she draws it up as a contract, the first thing anyone has ever signed with the Choir, and it will never be broken, only outlived. What it costs: many of the dead choose to go, and that's a second loss to live through, this time with goodbyes. The Keepers have to accept that what's preserved will change, which is the end of their faith. The first watch may never come home, and who stands it (Voss, Cael, Ione, Oskar, Orsolya's idiots, Okonkwo, the captain) is the last big choice. And it's forever: every people, every generation, sends singers, and some of them sit down. The first argument of the new council, about whether anyone can be made to go, never really ends. Afterward: the Beacon changes for the first time since before there were people: CREW ABOARD. PASS WITH CARE. The silver stops hunting. Some of the machines stay on, some, told at last that they may stop, simply stop, and some leave for somewhere no one has charted. The wires open, and a twelve-year-old who has checked every manifest for a year gets a call from her dad. The fleet builds a town in the empty berths, with schools, arguments and a bar run by a very tall Veshti. The Harbor was a mistranslation, and then they made it true. Some day, years on, a young officer comes up to the board and says the words to the captain.

endings.name: Say Good Morning
endings.gm: The stranger road, for a captain who's been past the lamp and can't stop thinking about it, or who has listened to Mother Orsolya too long. Everyone for a hundred thousand years has treated it as something to keep asleep. Nobody has ever tried to tell it that anyone is here. What it takes: people who've learned to be many without drowning: Ashael and the Lumen Circle (how to feel without being swallowed), the Echo (a mind that stayed plural), the Tessen children (the only native speakers), the Score rewritten from a lullaby into a greeting, Orsolya's one great working, and the whole Choir letting the song thin on purpose, which the Cantor will only do if the captain has earned more trust than anyone ever has, or forces it with the Tuner. Then someone stands at the lamp and says, in effect: you're asleep, and we aren't you, please mind your step. That's attunement or persuasion at nearly_impossible, with every ally and piece making it easier. It can't be tested first, and everyone will try to stop it: this is the one thing the Regent, the Admiral, the Abbess and the Cantor all agree on. What it costs: if it goes badly, the nearest worlds sit down on the first night and the fleet has a matter of hours. Run that as a desperate scramble for one of the other endings, not a game over. If it goes well it still costs whoever's at the lamp, who is probably never quite separate again, and the song ends, so the dead are let go, or go on with the Echo. Afterward: something the size of the sky is awake, and it's trying very hard to be careful. Nobody knows what it wants, and perhaps it doesn't either. About once a year everyone alive hears the same soft question, in no language, and the Tessen children, grown up now, are working on what it means. The Beacon has a new message, in a shaky hand: SOMEONE IS AWAKE. THEY'RE LEARNING. Nothing will ever be safe again, or lonely.

endings.name: The Regent's Peace
endings.gm: If the captain signs, hides, takes the succession or simply never goes, this is how the story ends without a last stand. The fleet survives, in a Hegemony berth or on a bad colony. People marry. The shipments go on, and perhaps it's the captain who stamps them now, doing sums in a white room. Other worlds learn the chimes, and more and more of the galaxy goes off watch, so the song gets no new verses and the sleep thins faster. Silent towns start on the frontier. Eleven years later a grown-up child from Tessen finds the captain and asks if they're ready now. If the player has a story left in them, the road is still open, at worse odds. If not, let them have those years, and make them good ones.
